Cardiovascular system.question: ১) Location of discontinuous capillaries excludes....?
Cardiovascular system.exp:
Discontinuous capillaries (sinusoidal capillaries) are characterized by large gaps between endothelial cells and a discontinuous basement membrane, allowing passage of large molecules and even cells. They are found in organs involved in filtration, storage, and exchange of blood cells, including the liver, spleen, and bone marrow. The lung contains mainly continuous capillaries, which have tight endothelial junctions and a continuous basement membrane to maintain an effective blood–air barrier required for gas exchange. Therefore, the lung is not a site of discontinuous capillaries.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Discontinuous capillaries (sinusoids) found in:

    • Liver

    • Spleen

    • Bone marrow

  • Continuous capillaries → Lung, muscle, CNS

  • Fenestrated capillaries → Kidney, endocrine glands, intestinal villi

Exam Pearl:
Sinusoidal capillaries are found in liver, spleen, and bone marrow—not in the lung.

Cardiovascular system.question: ২) Right or left coronary dominance is determined with the reference to the origin of which artery?
Cardiovascular system.exp:
Coronary artery dominance is determined by the artery that gives rise to the posterior interventricular artery (PIV/PDA), which supplies the posterior interventricular septum and inferior wall of the heart. In right dominant circulation, the posterior interventricular artery arises from the right coronary artery (RCA), which is the most common pattern. In left dominant circulation, it arises from the left circumflex artery (LCX). The anterior interventricular artery (LAD), circumflex artery, and marginal branches do not determine coronary dominance.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Coronary dominance is based on origin of posterior interventricular artery (PDA)

  • Right dominance → PDA from RCA (most common)

  • Left dominance → PDA from LCX

  • Coronary dominance affects blood supply to the inferior myocardium

Exam Pearl:
The origin of the posterior interventricular artery determines coronary dominance.

Cardiovascular system.question: ৩) Which vein doesn't drain into coronary sinus?
Cardiovascular system.exp:
Most veins of the heart drain into the coronary sinus, which then opens into the right atrium. Major tributaries of the coronary sinus include the great cardiac vein, middle cardiac vein, small cardiac vein, and posterior vein of the left ventricle. However, the anterior cardiac veins are an exception; they drain directly into the right atrium rather than passing through the coronary sinus. Therefore, the anterior cardiac vein does not drain into the coronary sinus.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Coronary sinus drains into: Right atrium

  • Tributaries of coronary sinus:

    • Great cardiac vein

    • Middle cardiac vein

    • Small cardiac vein

    • Posterior vein of left ventricle

  • Anterior cardiac veins → Directly drain into right atrium

Exam Pearl:
Anterior cardiac veins bypass the coronary sinus and open directly into the right atrium.

Cardiovascular system.question: ৪) Outflow tract of right ventricle develops from.....?
Cardiovascular system.exp:
The outflow tract of the right ventricle develops from the conus cordis, which is the proximal part of the embryonic bulbus cordis. The conus cordis forms the smooth-walled outflow regions of both ventricles: the infundibulum (conus arteriosus) of the right ventricle and the aortic vestibule of the left ventricle. The truncus arteriosus develops into the proximal parts of the aorta and pulmonary trunk. The primitive ventricle mainly contributes to the trabeculated part of the left ventricle.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Conus cordis → outflow tracts of ventricles

  • Right ventricle outflow tract → Infundibulum (conus arteriosus)

  • Truncus arteriosus → Aorta + pulmonary trunk

  • Primitive ventricle → mainly left ventricular trabeculated part

  • Bulbus cordis → contributes to right ventricle (trabeculated part) and outflow tract

Exam Pearl:
Right ventricular outflow tract (infundibulum) develops from conus cordis.

Cardiovascular system.question: ৫) Which is major determinant of systemic blood pressure?
Cardiovascular system.exp:
Arterioles are the major determinants of systemic blood pressure because they provide the greatest resistance to blood flow in the systemic circulation. Their smooth muscle walls can constrict or dilate, thereby regulating systemic vascular resistance (SVR) and controlling arterial pressure. According to the relationship, blood pressure is largely influenced by cardiac output and systemic vascular resistance. Capillaries are mainly involved in exchange of substances, venules in blood collection, and large arteries mainly act as conducting vessels and maintain pressure through elastic recoil.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Arterioles = resistance vessels

  • Main regulator of systemic vascular resistance

  • Vasoconstriction → ↑ blood pressure

  • Vasodilation → ↓ blood pressure

  • Capillaries → exchange vessels

Exam Pearl:
Arterioles are the primary determinants of sy

Cardiovascular system.question: ৬) Which arteries are called conducting arteries?
Cardiovascular system.exp:
Elastic arteries are called conducting arteries because they receive blood directly from the heart and distribute it to smaller arteries. They have a thick tunica media containing abundant elastic fibers, allowing them to stretch during ventricular systole and recoil during diastole, which helps maintain continuous blood flow and reduces pressure fluctuations. Examples include the aorta and its major branches. Muscular arteries are known as distributing arteries because they regulate blood flow to specific organs. Arterioles are resistance vessels that control systemic vascular resistance.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Elastic arteries = Conducting arteries

  • Example: Aorta, pulmonary trunk, large branches

  • Function: Maintain continuous blood flow by elastic recoil

  • Muscular arteries = Distributing arteries

  • Arterioles = Resistance vessels

Exam Pearl:
Conducting arteries are elastic arteries because of their ability to stretch and recoil.

Cardiovascular system.question: ৭) Which is the most common form of hypoxia?
Cardiovascular system.exp:
Hypoxic hypoxia is the most common form of hypoxia and occurs when there is a reduced partial pressure of oxygen (PaO₂) in arterial blood, leading to decreased oxygen availability to tissues. Common causes include high altitude, respiratory diseases causing impaired oxygen exchange, and airway obstruction. Anemic hypoxia occurs when oxygen-carrying capacity is reduced due to low hemoglobin levels. Stagnant hypoxia results from reduced blood flow, such as in heart failure or shock. Histotoxic hypoxia occurs when tissues cannot utilize oxygen despite adequate oxygen delivery, as in cyanide poisoning.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Types of hypoxia:

    • Hypoxic hypoxia → ↓ PaO₂

    • Anemic hypoxia → ↓ Hb

    • Stagnant hypoxia → ↓ blood flow

    • Histotoxic hypoxia → impaired cellular oxygen utilization

  • Most common type: Hypoxic hypoxia

Exam Pearl:
Reduced oxygen availability from low arterial oxygen tension causes the most common type of hypoxia: hypoxic hypoxia.

Cardiovascular system.question: ৮) Which organ gets maximum blood flow in ml/100gm/min?
Cardiovascular system.exp:
When considering blood flow per 100 grams of tissue (ml/100 g/min), the adrenal gland receives the highest blood flow among the given organs. The adrenal glands are highly vascular because steroid hormone synthesis requires a rich blood supply for rapid delivery of cholesterol precursors and transport of hormones. The kidney receives the highest total blood flow (about 20–25% of cardiac output) because of its large mass and filtration function, but its blood flow per unit weight is lower than the adrenal gland. The liver receives high total blood flow but lower flow per gram of tissue.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Highest blood flow per 100 g tissue → Adrenal gland

  • Highest total organ blood flow → Kidney

  • Kidney receives about 20–25% of cardiac output

  • Adrenal gland has rich vascular supply for hormone secretion

  • Brain and heart also have high metabolic blood flow demands

Exam Pearl:
Maximum blood flow per gram of tissue = Adrenal gland; maximum total blood flow = Kidney.

Cardiovascular system.question: ৯) What is the basis of Korotkoff's sound?
Cardiovascular system.exp:
Korotkoff sounds are the sounds heard during blood pressure measurement with a sphygmomanometer. They are produced due to turbulent blood flow in a partially compressed artery, usually the brachial artery. When cuff pressure is between systolic and diastolic pressure, blood intermittently passes through the narrowed artery during systole, creating turbulence and producing Korotkoff sounds. When cuff pressure falls below diastolic pressure, the artery remains open throughout the cardiac cycle, blood flow becomes laminar, and the sounds disappear. Arterial expansion and valve closure sounds are not responsible for Korotkoff sounds.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Korotkoff sounds → Turbulent blood flow

  • Measured by: Sphygmomanometer

  • First Korotkoff sound → Systolic BP

  • Disappearance of sounds (Phase V) → Diastolic BP

  • Site commonly used: Brachial artery

Exam Pearl:
Korotkoff sounds are due to turbulence in a partially compressed artery.

Cardiovascular system.question: ১০) What is the amount of blood pumped out by each ventricle during each beat?
Cardiovascular system.exp:
Stroke volume (SV) is the amount of blood pumped out by each ventricle during each heartbeat. It is calculated as the difference between end-diastolic volume (EDV) and end-systolic volume (ESV). In a healthy adult at rest, stroke volume is approximately 70 mL per beat. Cardiac output refers to the total amount of blood pumped by the heart per minute and is calculated as heart rate × stroke volume. Cardiac index is cardiac output adjusted for body surface area, while ejection fraction represents the percentage of ventricular blood volume ejected during systole.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Stroke volume = Blood ejected per beat

  • Formula: SV = EDV − ESV

  • Cardiac output = Heart rate × Stroke volume

  • Normal ejection fraction: approximately 55–70%

  • Left ventricular stroke volume determines systemic cardiac output

Exam Pearl:
Blood pumped by one ventricle in one heartbeat = Stroke volume.

Cardiovascular system.question: ১১) Which is the value of normal plasma colloid osmotic pressure (mmHg)?
Cardiovascular system.exp:
The normal plasma colloid osmotic pressure (COP), also known as plasma oncotic pressure, is approximately 28 mmHg. It is mainly generated by plasma proteins, especially albumin, which help retain fluid within the intravascular space and oppose capillary hydrostatic pressure. A decrease in plasma protein levels, particularly albumin (as in nephrotic syndrome or liver disease), reduces colloid osmotic pressure and can lead to edema formation. The other values represent much lower pressures and do not correspond to normal plasma oncotic pressure.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Plasma colloid osmotic pressure: ≈ 28 mmHg

  • Major contributor: Albumin

  • Function: Maintains fluid within blood vessels

  • Decreased oncotic pressure → edema

  • Capillary hydrostatic pressure promotes fluid filtration out of vessels

Exam Pearl:
Normal plasma oncotic pressure is about 28 mmHg, mainly due to albumin.

Cardiovascular system.question: ১২) Which is the commonest aetiology of chronic ischemic heart disease?
Cardiovascular system.exp:
The most common cause of chronic ischemic heart disease (IHD) is atherosclerosis of the coronary arteries. Atherosclerotic plaque formation causes progressive narrowing of coronary arteries, reducing myocardial blood supply, especially during increased oxygen demand, leading to stable angina and chronic myocardial ischemia. Congenital coronary stenosis is rare, coronary vasospasm is associated with variant (Prinzmetal) angina, and coronary embolism is an uncommon cause of myocardial ischemia. Therefore, atherosclerosis is the primary underlying pathology responsible for chronic ischemic heart disease.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Commonest cause of chronic IHD → Coronary atherosclerosis

  • Atherosclerotic plaque → narrowing of coronary arteries

  • Stable angina → fixed coronary obstruction

  • Vasospasm → Prinzmetal (variant) angina

  • Major risk factors: Hypertension, diabetes mellitus, smoking, dyslipidemia

Exam Pearl:
Chronic ischemic heart disease is most commonly caused by coronary atherosclerosis.

Cardiovascular system.question: ১৩) Which is most common form of angina?
Cardiovascular system.exp:
The most common form of angina pectoris is stable angina, which occurs due to a fixed atherosclerotic narrowing of coronary arteries. It is characterized by predictable chest pain or discomfort that occurs with exertion or emotional stress and is relieved by rest or nitrates. Unstable angina results from acute plaque disruption with partial thrombosis and is part of acute coronary syndrome. Prinzmetal (variant) angina is caused by coronary vasospasm and typically occurs at rest. Crescendo angina is a type of unstable angina with progressively increasing frequency or severity.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Most common angina → Stable angina

  • Cause → Fixed coronary artery obstruction

  • Trigger → Exercise/stress

  • Relief → Rest or nitrates

  • Prinzmetal angina → Coronary vasospasm at rest

Exam Pearl:
Stable angina is the commonest type of angina due to fixed atherosclerotic coronary narrowing.

Cardiovascular system.question: ১৪) Which is the most sensitive & specific biomarker of myocardial damage?
Cardiovascular system.exp:
Cardiac troponin I is considered one of the most sensitive and specific biomarkers for myocardial damage and is the preferred biomarker for diagnosing myocardial infarction (MI). It is released into the blood when cardiac myocytes are injured due to ischemia and necrosis. Troponin I is highly specific to cardiac muscle and remains elevated for several days after myocardial injury. CK-MB is also useful, especially for detecting reinfarction, but it is less specific because it can rise with skeletal muscle injury. LDH and AST are older, less specific markers of myocardial injury.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Best biomarker for MI → Cardiac troponins (Troponin I/T)

  • Troponin rises: 3–6 hours after injury

  • Remains elevated: 7–10 days (approximately)

  • CK-MB → useful for reinfarction detection

  • AST and LDH → older, non-specific markers

Exam Pearl:
Troponin I is the most sensitive and specific biomarker for myocardial damage.

Cardiovascular system.question: ১৫) Which is a minor criteria for diagnosis of rheumatic fever?
Cardiovascular system.exp:
According to the Jones criteria for diagnosis of acute rheumatic fever, polyarthralgia is a minor criterion. The major criteria include carditis, migratory polyarthritis, Sydenham chorea, erythema marginatum, and subcutaneous nodules. Minor criteria include fever, arthralgia (polyarthralgia), elevated inflammatory markers (ESR/CRP), and prolonged PR interval on ECG. Carditis, chorea, and erythema marginatum are major manifestations of rheumatic fever, not minor criteria.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Jones major criteria:

    • Carditis

    • Migratory polyarthritis

    • Chorea

    • Erythema marginatum

    • Subcutaneous nodules

  • Minor criteria:

    • Polyarthralgia

    • Fever

    • Raised ESR/CRP

    • Prolonged PR interval

  • Diagnosis requires evidence of preceding Group A Streptococcal infection

Exam Pearl:
Polyarthralgia is a minor Jones criterion; carditis, chorea, and erythema marginatum are major criteria.

Cardiovascular system.question: ১৬) Which is most common form of cardiomyopathy?
Cardiovascular system.exp:
The most common form of cardiomyopathy overall is ischemic cardiomyopathy, which results from coronary artery disease causing myocardial ischemia and infarction, leading to impaired ventricular function. Among the primary (non-ischemic) cardiomyopathies, dilated cardiomyopathy is the most common type. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is characterized by left ventricular hypertrophy, while restrictive cardiomyopathy is the least common and involves impaired ventricular filling due to increased myocardial stiffness. Therefore, for a general question asking the most common form of cardiomyopathy, ischemic cardiomyopathy is the accepted answer.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Most common overall cardiomyopathy → Ischemic cardiomyopathy

  • Most common primary cardiomyopathy → Dilated cardiomyopathy

  • Dilated CM → systolic dysfunction, reduced ejection fraction

  • Hypertrophic CM → diastolic dysfunction, asymmetric septal hypertrophy

  • Restrictive CM → impaired ventricular filling

Exam Pearl:
Ischemic cardiomyopathy is the commonest overall; dilated cardiomyopathy is the commonest primary cardiomyopathy.

Cardiovascular system.question: ১৭) Which is the most common cause of death in 1st few hours following MI?
Cardiovascular system.exp:
The most common cause of death in the first few hours following myocardial infarction (MI) is cardiac arrhythmia, especially ventricular fibrillation (VF). Acute myocardial ischemia causes electrical instability of the myocardium, leading to life-threatening ventricular arrhythmias that can result in sudden cardiac death. Myocardial failure (heart failure/cardiogenic shock) may occur after extensive infarction but is usually a later complication. Cardiac tamponade can occur due to free wall rupture, typically several days after MI, and mural thrombosis is a later complication due to endocardial damage and stasis.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Early death after MI → Arrhythmia (especially ventricular fibrillation)

  • Cardiogenic shock → due to extensive myocardial damage

  • Free wall rupture → may cause cardiac tamponade

  • Mural thrombus → risk of systemic embolism

  • First hours are dominated by electrical complications

Exam Pearl:
First few hours after MI: think ventricular arrhythmia as the commonest cause of death.

Cardiovascular system.question: ১৮) Which is criteria of non cardiac chest pain?
Cardiovascular system.exp:
Non-cardiac chest pain is often characterized by diffuse, poorly localized pain that does not follow a typical cardiac pattern. Cardiac chest pain (such as angina) is usually described as a central, constricting discomfort that is precipitated by exertion or emotional stress and may be associated with breathlessness. Localized chest pain, especially a sharp pain that can be pointed to with one finger, is more suggestive of a non-cardiac cause. Therefore, among the given options, diffuse pain is the best criterion for non-cardiac chest pain.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Non-cardiac chest pain:

    • Diffuse or poorly localized

    • Sharp/variable character

    • May not be related to exertion

  • Cardiac chest pain:

    • Central chest discomfort

    • Triggered by exertion

    • May radiate to arm/jaw

    • Associated with dyspnea or sweating

Exam Pearl:
Diffuse, poorly localized chest pain favors a non-cardiac origin.

Cardiovascular system.question: ১৯) Features of right heart failure excludes...?
Cardiovascular system.exp:
The typical features of right heart failure (RHF) are due to systemic venous congestion, including raised jugular venous pressure (JVP), hepatomegaly, peripheral edema, and ascites. Cardiomegaly is not a specific feature of right heart failure; it may occur in many cardiac conditions, including both right and left ventricular enlargement, but it is not a hallmark sign of venous congestion. Therefore, among the given options, cardiomegaly is the best answer as an excluded feature.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Right heart failure → Systemic venous congestion

  • Signs:

    • Raised JVP

    • Hepatomegaly

    • Ascites

    • Peripheral edema

  • Left heart failure → pulmonary congestion:

    • Dyspnea

    • Orthopnea

    • Pulmonary edema

  • Cardiomegaly can occur in various cardiac diseases

Exam Pearl:
Raised JVP, hepatomegaly, and ascites are classic signs of right heart failure; cardiomegaly is not specific.

Cardiovascular system.question: ২০) Which investigation is done to assess risk in heart failure?
Cardiovascular system.exp:
Echocardiography is the key investigation used to assess prognosis and risk in heart failure. It evaluates important parameters such as left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF), ventricular size, wall motion abnormalities, and valvular function, which help determine severity and guide treatment. BNP is useful for diagnosis and assessing severity of heart failure but is not the primary investigation for risk stratification. Serum electrolytes are monitored for complications and treatment effects, especially with diuretics and ACE inhibitors, while thyroid function may identify reversible causes of heart failure.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Best investigation to assess heart failure severity/risk → Echocardiography

  • Important parameter: Left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF)

  • BNP → diagnosis and prognosis marker

  • Electrolytes → monitor treatment complications

  • Reduced EF suggests systolic heart failure

Exam Pearl:
Echocardiography is the main investigation for assessing risk and severity in heart failure.

Cardiovascular system.question: ২১) Which is the most effective drug for preventing AF?
Cardiovascular system.exp:
Amiodarone is considered one of the most effective drugs for prevention of atrial fibrillation (AF) recurrence because of its broad antiarrhythmic activity. It is a Class III antiarrhythmic drug that blocks potassium channels and prolongs the cardiac action potential and refractory period, helping maintain sinus rhythm. However, its use is limited by significant long-term adverse effects such as thyroid dysfunction, pulmonary fibrosis, liver toxicity, and corneal deposits. Beta blockers and diltiazem are mainly used for rate control in AF, while digoxin is useful for rate control in selected patients, especially with heart failure, but is less effective for rhythm maintenance.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Most effective antiarrhythmic for AF prevention → Amiodarone

  • Class → Class III potassium channel blocker

  • Major adverse effects:

    • Thyroid dysfunction

    • Pulmonary fibrosis

    • Hepatotoxicity

    • Corneal deposits

  • Beta blockers/diltiazem → Rate control drugs

Exam Pearl:
Amiodarone is the most effective drug for maintaining sinus rhythm and preventing AF recurrence.

Cardiovascular system.question: ২২) Which is the cardinal symptom of ACS?
Cardiovascular system.exp:
The cardinal symptom of acute coronary syndrome (ACS) is chest pain (anginal pain). It is typically described as a central, heavy, constricting, or squeezing discomfort behind the sternum, often radiating to the left arm, neck, jaw, or epigastrium. It occurs due to myocardial ischemia caused by reduced coronary blood flow. Breathlessness, vomiting, and collapse may occur as associated symptoms, especially in severe MI or high-risk patients, but they are not the primary or cardinal symptom. Some patients, particularly elderly or diabetic patients, may present with atypical symptoms.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Cardinal symptom of ACS → Chest pain

  • Typical pain: Retrosternal, pressure-like, radiating

  • Cause → Myocardial ischemia

  • Associated symptoms:

    • Sweating

    • Nausea/vomiting

    • Dyspnea

  • Atypical presentation common in diabetes and elderly patients

Exam Pearl:
Chest pain is the hallmark symptom of acute coronary syn

Cardiovascular system.question: ২৩) If once Streptokinase is given, how long the person needn't to be given it again?
Cardiovascular system.exp:
After administration of streptokinase, repeat use is generally avoided for 5 years because the drug is derived from β-hemolytic streptococci and can stimulate the formation of anti-streptokinase antibodies. These antibodies may neutralize the effect of subsequent doses and increase the risk of allergic reactions, including anaphylaxis. Therefore, if thrombolysis is required again within this period, another fibrinolytic agent such as a tissue plasminogen activator (tPA) is preferred.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Streptokinase → Fibrinolytic thrombolytic drug

  • Derived from → Streptococci

  • Repeat administration avoided for → 5 years

  • Reason → Antibody formation + allergic reaction risk

  • Alternative thrombolytics → Alteplase, tenecteplase

Exam Pearl:
After one dose of streptokinase, avoid repeating it for 5 years due to antibody-mediated resistance and allergy risk.

Cardiovascular system.question: ২৪) On auscultation of precordium of a patient you found - loud 1st heart sound, opening snap & mid diastolic murmur. what may be most possible diagnosis?
Cardiovascular system.exp:
The combination of loud first heart sound (S1), opening snap, and mid-diastolic murmur is the classic auscultatory finding of mitral stenosis (MS). In MS, narrowing of the mitral valve causes increased left atrial pressure and delayed valve opening. The sudden opening of a stenotic mitral valve produces an opening snap, followed by a mid-diastolic rumbling murmur best heard at the apex. A loud S1 occurs due to forceful closure of a still-mobile stenotic mitral valve. Aortic stenosis causes an ejection systolic murmur, tricuspid regurgitation causes pansystolic murmur, and mitral regurgitation causes pansystolic murmur with a soft S1.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Mitral stenosis:

    • Loud S1

    • Opening snap

    • Mid-diastolic rumbling murmur

    • Best heard at apex

  • Common cause: Rheumatic heart disease

  • Opening snap interval decreases with severe MS

  • MR → pansystolic murmur, soft S1

Exam Pearl:
Loud S1 + opening snap + mid-diastolic murmur = Mitral stenosis.

Cardiovascular system.question: ২৫) Which hormone decrease arterial blood pressure?
Cardiovascular system.exp:
Bradykinin is a vasoactive peptide that causes decrease in arterial blood pressure by producing potent vasodilation through stimulation of nitric oxide (NO) and prostacyclin release from vascular endothelium. It increases vascular permeability and contributes to inflammatory responses. Adrenaline generally increases blood pressure by increasing cardiac output and causing vasoconstriction (α₁ effect), although β₂ effects may cause vasodilation at low doses. Thyroxine increases metabolic activity and may increase cardiac output, while aldosterone increases sodium and water retention, leading to increased blood volume and blood pressure.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Bradykinin → Vasodilation → ↓ arterial BP

  • ACE inhibitors increase bradykinin levels → cough and angioedema

  • Aldosterone → Na⁺ and water retention → ↑ BP

  • Adrenaline → mainly ↑ BP

  • Nitric oxide → important vasodilator

Exam Pearl:
Bradykinin is a natural vasodilator that lowers arterial blood pressure.
